YOUTUBE SHORTS WORKFLOW

The workflow this page is built for

A Short has very little time to earn attention and deliver a complete payoff. The script needs a clear promise in the first three seconds, short spoken lines, and a finish that does not feel rushed. CuePrompt turns that timing plan into a readable recording workflow.

From hook to vertical export

  1. Choose the YouTube Shorts template, define one viewer problem, and write the promised result before the explanation.
  2. Split the script into a 0–3 second hook, a compact explanation, a visible payoff, and one next action.
  3. Rehearse against a 60-second target, record vertically, then review the first frame, captions, and ending before export.

Recommended CuePrompt settings

  • Use large text, short lines, and a slightly faster but still conversational scroll.
  • Record in 9:16 and keep your face and important visuals inside the center safe area.
  • Add [pause] before the payoff and leave a clean beat at the end for editing or a loop.

A short-video structure that fits

0–3s promise → problem in one line → two or three fast steps → visible result → next-video or subscribe action.

“Your script is not too long—it starts too slowly. [pause] Put the result first, explain only the two steps viewers need, and save the background for a longer video.”

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Spending the opening seconds introducing yourself instead of stating the result.
  • Packing multiple unrelated tips into one Short.
  • Ending immediately after the final word with no room for captions, a cut, or a loop.

Questions before you record

Must every Short be exactly 60 seconds?

No. Use the shortest length that delivers the promised result, then verify the current YouTube upload rules before publishing.

How can I make the first frame stronger?

Start with the result, a specific question, or a visible before-and-after. Avoid greetings that delay the reason to keep watching.

Can CuePrompt help with a seamless loop?

Yes. Write an ending that naturally leads back to the opening line and leave a short editing beat at both ends.
